newsitem.title: FRANCE: France dismisses EMU budget speculation.
newsitem.headline: France dismisses EMU budget speculation.

text.p: The French government on Thursday dismissed mounting media speculation about its ability to reduce the public deficit enough to pass the fitness test for joining a single euro currency, and vowed to do all that was necessary.

In an apparent bid to nip speculation in the bud, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis issued a statement saying France was set on cutting the 1997 deficit to three percent of gross domestic product, as required for European economic and monetary union.
"In any case, the government will take sufficient steps to respect its target for the public deficit of three percent of GDP in 1997, if necessary," the statement said.

In the warm-up for a May parliamentary debate on what is set to be another thrifty budget for 1998, the press is questioning whether the government will have to do more than planned to get the deficit down to three percent of national wealth this year.
Arthuis's statement followed similar declarations earlier in the day by government spokesman Alain Lamassoure.

And it came shortly after a story in afternoon daily Le Monde saying the budget division of the finance ministry had produced a confidential "forecast note" which said the 1997 deficit could hit 3.5 percent of GDP, taking account of the cutbacks so far planned.

The newspaper said, however, that the ministry division had the task of enumerating all the possible risks of overshoot and that there was also a scenario which saw the 1997 deficit at 3.3 percent of GDP if there were firm growth and better revenues.
Part of the "worst scenario" calculation for this year was a social security deficit of 47 billion francs ($8.1 billion), 17 billion more than planned.
In a similar vein, 1998's deficit could hit 4.5 percent, or four percent including corrective steps, again including a hefty social security deficit of 58 billion francs, the paper said.
Arthuis pointed out that the budget deficit for the first two months of this year had come 17.6 billion francs lower than the 90 billion francs deficit at the same stage last year.
He reiterated that the economy was forecast to grow at least 2.3 percent this year, reason for greater confidence than last year, when GDP grew by a modest 1.3 percent.
Lamassoure told RTL radio earlier that the government had mastered spending "like has never been done" and the social security system's spending was also being reined in.
"If we were to note during the year that revenues were not coming in fast enough, then we would have to take additional measures. But we already have a margin of manoeuvre," he said.
Arthuis and Lamassoure both highlighted that the government had already decided to freeze 10 billion francs more in spending credits for this year since unveiling its initial 1997 budget.

"If it turned out that there were any reasons to prompt us to make further savings, we would go further. Last year we froze 20 billion (extra spending credits), we can go further this year," Lamassoure said.

Nevertheless, several newspapers have been highlighting the risks of weak tax receipts and other revenue shortfalls making it hard to cut the social security deficit to the 30 billion francs ($5.2 billion) which the government is counting on.

Talk of budget troubles combined with continuing talk that a government reshuffle or dissolution of parliament sent a ripple of concern through French government debt markets on Thursday, though some economists played down the matter.
"It was a combination of the deficit (reports), which I think is a bit silly, and politics," ABN Amro Finance economist Philippe Brossard said.

Parliament is due to discuss the 1998 budget in mid-May. After using a transer of 37.5 billion francs from France Telecom in its 1997 budget and deficit calculations, the pressure is on to find similar resources to cut the deficit further next year. ($ = 5.810 French Francs)
